power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA.

We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study.
In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates.
Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone.

In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years.
Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH.
Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by neurodegeneration and a progressive decline in cognitive function, with structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) playing a central role in quantifying disease-relevant brain atrophy. 1 MRI-derived cortical thickness (cTH) and volume are widely used markers of neurodegeneration in AD and related dementias (ADRD), 2 providing non-invasive measures of cortical atrophy.

text.text: Cortical surface area (cSA) has received comparatively less attention in aging and dementia research, despite cortical volume being a composite measure of both cTH and cSA, two metrics reflecting distinct dimensions of cortical morphology. cSA has been linked to cognition and intelligence across the lifespan [7] [8] [9] and has been shown in some populations to have stronger influence on cortical volume than cTH. 10, 11 Developmental models link cortical surface expansion to progenitor proliferation and tangential expansion of cortical columns, whereas cTH reflects radial growth and layer formation within the cortical sheet. 12, 13 Twin and genetic studies of adolescent participants further demonstrate that cSA and cTH are highly heritable but genetically distinct. 10, 14, 15 Together, these findings indicate that volume combines separable sources of biological variation, and evaluating these dimensions separately may provide a more precise framework for interpreting cortical morphometry in brain aging than volume or cTH alone.

The original goal of ADNI was to test whether serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), other biological markers, and clinical and neuropsychological assessment can be combined to measure the progression of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and early Alzheimer's disease (AD).
The National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) was established in 1999 by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and serves as the centralized data repository for the ADRCs.

NACC and ADNI were used as large multisite aging and AD cohorts to evaluate cross-sectional diagnostic associations and progression to incident AD. 20, 21 CAM was included as a single-centre, vascular-enriched cohort to evaluate demographic and vascular disease associations with . morphometry in participants enriched for extracranial carotid atherosclerotic disease (ECAD) and vascular risk. text.text: All analyses were conducted independently in NACC, ADNI and CAM.
Correlations between cSA and cTH were assessed within each cohort using Spearman correlation.
Demographic associations with cSA and cTH were evaluated using multivariable linear regression models.
Association of cSA and cTH with MCI and ADRD were evaluated using cross-sectional multivariable logistic regression comparing CU vs.
MCI and ADRD as outcomes.

All models were adjusted for age, sex, years of education, race, ethnicity, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 carrier status; ADNI models additionally included magnetic field strength and image pre-processing status. β estimates for all regression models were standardized.

In models estimating risk associated with lower morphometrics, measures were multiplied by -1 so that odds/hazard ratios greater than 1 reflected higher odds/hazard per 1standard deviation lower morphometric value.

Secondary models were performed using the DMN as a regional composite, and ADNI sensitivity analyses were performed restricting the sample to participants whose morphometrics were derived from 3T, un-processed imaging.

To evaluate cross-sectional cSA/cTH phenotypes, NACC and ADNI cohort-specific lower-quartile thresholds were used to classify participants as normal cSA/normal cTH, normal cSA/low cTH, low cSA/normal cTH, and low cSA/low cTH, with "low" defining values below the threshold, and "normal" defining values above the lower-quartile threshold.
This was performed instead of using the highest quartile to define "normal" in order to maximize sample size.
Similar was done to delineate high/low volume.
Multivariable logistic regressions were used to evaluate the association of morphometric phenotypes with MCI and ADRD compared to CU using normal cSA/normal cTH as the reference factor.
Additional models were assessed exchanging the reference factor to assess differences between phenotype groups.
To assess cross-sectional discrimination across phenotypes, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed for CU vs.
ADRD.
Associations of baseline cSA and cTH to incident ADRD were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models among ADNI participants who were CU or MCI at baseline.
The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using scaled Schoenfeld residuals for each model.
Time-to-event was defined as time from baseline MRI to first observed ADRD diagnosis.
Participants who did not progress to ADRD were censored at the last available MRI follow-up visit date.
All Cox models included age, sex, education, race, ethnicity, APOE ε4 carrier status, magnetic field strength and imaging preprocessing status as covariates.
Nested Cox models were used to assess whether cSA provided incremental prognostic information beyond cTH and whether decomposed morphometry outperformed cortical volume.

Likelihood ratio tests compared nested models including covariates alone (age, sex, education, race, ethnicity, APOE ε4 carriage, magnet strength, image preprocessing status), covariates plus cSA, covariates plus cTH, covariates plus volume, covariates plus cSA and cTH, and covariates plus cSA, cTH, and volume.
Model performance was summarized using Akaike information criterion (AIC) and Harrel C-index.
Optimized cSA, cTH, and volume cutoffs were derived within the longitudinal ADNI cohort using ROC curve analyses among participants who were CU/MCI at baseline.
For each measure, ROC curves were used to evaluate the discrimination of incident ADRD.
Optimal thresholds were defined using Youden's J statistic.
Participants were classified as having normal/low cSA, cTH, and volume, based on the threshold maximizing Youden's J statistic.
Binary cSA/cTH classifications were combined into four phenotypes: normal cSA/normal cTH, normal cSA/low cTH, low cSA/normal cTH, and low cSA/low cTH which were used in subsequent survival analyses.
Kaplan-Meier curves were generated for normal/low cSA, normal/low cTH, normal/low volume, and combined cSA/cTH phenotype groups, with differences assessed using log-rank tests.
Statistical significance was defined as P<.05 in all analyses.

text.text: The majority of ADRD structural neuroimaging studies to date have focused on cTH and volume, reflecting strong historical evidence that ADRD is associated with cortical thinning and regional atrophy. 3, 5, [41] [42] [43] Although cortical volume is a composite measure of cSA and cTH, few studies have evaluated cSA as an independent factor of cortical vulnerability.

text.text: In this multi-cohort study across vascular-enriched and memory clinic cohorts, we demonstrated that cSA in the AD-Signature and DMN regions provide clinically relevant information not captured by cTH or volume alone.
Lower cSA was independently associated with MCI and ADRD cross-sectionally and predicted incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years.

Moreover, individuals with both low cSA and low cTH showed the greatest clinical vulnerability i.e., the highest risk for MCI and ADRD, supporting the value of decomposing cortical volume into its component dimensions.
Together, the results of this study suggest that cortical vulnerability in ADRD is better represented when evaluating cSA in addition to cTH.

Multiple aspects of our data support conceptualization and evaluation of cSA and cTH as highly independent morphometric features that may reflect distinct biological vulnerabilities. cSA and cTH were only weakly correlated in all three cohorts, and both metrics showed independent associations with MCI, ADRD, and incident ADRD.
The proteomics analyses also support this concept through demonstration of distinct cellular and molecular pathways in cSA and cTH.

Although cSA has not been as well studied in the aging and dementia fields, evaluating cSA as an independent feature of brain morphometry is in keeping with developmental biology studies that have shown cSA and cTH are highly heritable traits with distinct genetic pathways. 10, 14, 15 Moreover, these findings are consistent with evolutionary and developmental studies that have shown greater cSA is associated with higher intelligence and cognitive ability in humans [7] [8] [9] and with mammalian studies suggesting that evolutionary expansion of cSA supports greater cognitive capacity across species. 44, 45 Together, these findings underscore that cSA, like cTH, represents a fundamental and unique dimension of cortical architecture.

text.text: From a clinical perspective, combined cSA/cTH phenotyping may provide a practical framework for morphometric risk stratification.

Cortical volume and cTH are commonly used for prognostication of dementia risk, however our data suggest that evaluating cSA and cTH together improves identification of individuals at greater risk for clinical progression.
Participants with low cSA and low cTH had the poorest ADRD-free survival and the highest risk of incident ADRD than either morphometric dimension alone.

One possible interpretation is that low cSA may reflect a more developmentally constrained or premorbid dimension of cortical vulnerability, where low cTH may more closely reflect active neurodegenerative tissue loss.

Under this framework, the low cSA/low cTH phenotype may represent a subgroup with more extensive or multifactorial cortical damage, helping explain its stronger association with ADRD progression than either metric alone.
The added value of cSA/cTH phenotyping may reflect, in part, the limitations of cortical volume as a composite measure.

Because volume reflects both dimensions, similar volumetric values can arise from different cSA/cTH profiles that may not carry the same biological or clinical meaning; collapsing these into a single aggregate volume measure may mask this separable morphometric information.

Consistent with this interpretation, models incorporating both cSA and cTH demonstrated better prognostic performance than models using cTH or volume alone and adding volume to a cSA+cTH model did not significantly improve model fit.

Mathematically, the combined measure may also disproportionally reflect whichever dimension accounts for more variance, and it has been suggested that more interindividual variation in cortical volume is attributed to cSA rather than cTH. 10, 11 Furthermore, a composite measure makes it difficult to distinguish additive versus combined interactive effects that may hinder causal inference if cSA and cTH have different associations with the outcome of interest.

Risk factor analyses further suggest that cSA and cTH may not be equally sensitive to all sources of dementia risk.

text.text: Notably, carotid disease in CAM participants was associated with significantly lower cSA, but not cTH, highlighting a potentially distinct pattern related to cerebrovascular disease.

These distinctions are interesting because they indicate hypertension, APOE ε4 allele presence, age, and carotid stenosis may influence cortical structure through different mechanisms or timescales, and these differences highlight the benefit of assessing both cSA and cTH and the need for further research into cSA/cTH interactions.

Because ADNI and NACC do not evaluate large vessel cerebrovascular disease, the extent to which carotid stenosis or other measures of vascular burden contribute to cortical morphometry in these cohorts remains unknown and will require further investigation.

text.text: Several methodological features relevant to prior gaps in the literature add to the rigor of this study.
First, the use of a large sample drawn from three separate cohorts increases generalizability and reduces concern that the findings reflect cohort or acquisition/processingspecific biases.
However, not every analysis could be performed with each dataset due to cohort-specific limitations in variable of interest availability.

Second, cSA and cTH were examined within a priori AD-Signature and DMN brain region composites rather than through unconstrained regional testing across the whole cortex reducing multiple-comparison burden and grounding the analysis in regions with established ADRD vulnerability.
Third, longitudinal analyses with up to 15-year follow-up provide evidence that baseline cSA relates to future clinical progression.
Finally, CSF proteomic analyses offer biological context for the distinct associations seen in cSA and cTH.
This study also has several limitations.
1) The observational design precludes causal inference, and lower cSA/cTH may reflect preexisting vulnerability or other accumulated disease-related differences.
2) Although models were adjusted for key demographic, genetic, and imaging covariates, residual confounding of comorbidities and other cohort-specific characteristics remains possible.
3) Morphometric estimates rely on FreeSurfer segmentation accuracy, which may be dependent on participant age and post-processing protocols 32 .
4) Normal/low phenotypes are useful for visualization and risk stratification but are cohortderived and should thus be interpreted as pragmatic summaries rather than fixed biological . thresholds.
5) Our longitudinal analyses show that baseline cSA and cTH predict future clinical progression, but do not assess cSA or cTH over time.
Future studies could determine whether cSA is primarily a vulnerability marker, dynamic disease marker, or both.

6) Analyses did not separately evaluate progression from CU to MCI and MCI to ADRD or stratify these transitions by evidence of amyloid pathology; therefore, incremental prognostic value of cSA beyond cortical volume, APOE ε4, and baseline cognition within biomarkerdefined clinical subgroups remains uncertain.

Future studies incorporating longitudinal morphometric measurements, stage-and biomarker-specific analyses, and independent replication are needed to address these limitations and further clarify the biological and prognostic significance of cSA.
In conclusion, these findings support cSA as a clinically relevant dimension of cortical morphology.
Future studies should consider decomposing cortical volume into cSA and cTH to better characterize distinct and complementary patterns of cortical vulnerability.

Incorporating cSA into ADRD neuroimaging frameworks may improve risk stratification, clarify heterogeneous pathways towards dementia, and provide a stronger morphometric bridge to studies of neurodegeneration.
